sources.excerpt: Keratoconjunctivitis Clinical Evaluation In classic presentations, patients complain of eyelids sticking together on waking. They may describe itching and burning or a gritty, foreign-body sensation. Pus sliding across the eye may distort vision, although visual acuity is normal. Photophobia is minimal. Family members with similar complaints typically present with conjunctivitis from an infectious cause. sources.excerpt: blindness associated with facial trauma. Emergent decompressive surgery may be sight-saving in patients with severe symptoms. Significant evidence shows that long-term outcomes correlate with time to intervention in patients with severe AOCS. Half of patients presenting with decreased visual acuity due to retrobulbar hematoma experience immediate resolution of symptoms with emergent decompression. Irreversible visual loss can be expected with retinal ischemia that lasts longer than 120 minutes, although some patients may experience partial recovery with decompression outside this window.

Of patients with CNS involvement from infective endocarditis, one third had completely normal cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), one fourth had a slightly abnormal CSF but an aseptic culture, and one fourth had frankly purulent CSF. diseases.name: Conjunctivitis
diseases.rationale: The questionnaire asks about red eyes, discharge, and precipitating events like infection, which align with symptoms of conjunctivitis such as eyelids sticking together, itching, burning, and a gritty sensation. A history of a recent upper respiratory infection is also noted as being associated with viral causes.

diseases.name: Dry Eye Disease
diseases.rationale: The questionnaire addresses symptoms like eye pain, redness, and blurry vision. These overlap with common complaints of Dry Eye Disease (Keratoconjunctivitis Sicca), which include a foreign-body sensation, burning, itching, redness (hyperemia), and blurry vision that may improve with blinking.

diseases.name: Orbital Compartment Syndrome
diseases.rationale: The questionnaire asks about trauma, vision loss, and eye pain. These are critical symptoms for Acute Orbital Compartment Syndrome (AOCS), a condition that can follow facial trauma and lead to permanent blindness if not treated promptly. AOCS is a common cause of blindness associated with facial trauma.

diseases.name: Stroke
diseases.rationale: The questionnaire includes questions about sudden onset, vision loss, blurry vision, double vision (diplopia), and headache. These are recognized as common signs and symptoms of an ischemic stroke, which can present with monocular or binocular visual loss, visual field deficits, and diplopia.

diseases.name: Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus
diseases.rationale: The questionnaire asks about facial rash and various eye symptoms like pain, redness, and vision changes. Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (HZO) can manifest with ocular symptoms such as keratitis, iritis, and retinitis, as well as neurologic complications like optic neuritis. The presence of a facial rash is a key diagnostic clue.

diseases.name: Orbital Cellulitis
diseases.rationale: The questionnaire asks about infection, eye pain, and redness. Orbital cellulitis is mentioned as a potential differential diagnosis for central nervous system sequelae of infectious endocarditis, indicating it is a relevant condition to consider in the context of eye problems potentially linked to infection.

review_notes.note: The questionnaire includes red flag symptoms such as diplopia, severe headache, and focal neurologic deficits. These can be associated with serious conditions like stroke or syncope and require careful evaluation.

A history of trauma preceding eye symptoms is a critical finding, as it can be associated with Acute Orbital Compartment Syndrome, which may require emergent intervention to prevent permanent vision loss.
